items.summary: The Network of Women in Media, India (NWMI) has told the Supreme Court that Delhi Police’s counter-affidavit, far from rebutting allegations of harassment of journalists at the anti-SIR protests, “itself reveals the extent of the interference complained of”. In a rejoinder filed on November 21, NWMI said paragraphs of the affidavit “read like a catalogue of admissions” and that terms such as “mistaken identity”, “verification” and “merely removed” and “released upon identification” are euphemisms “deployed to soften the description of actual restraint”. The NWMI’s original petition is one of several filed in the Supreme Court by journalists’ bodies, which allege that the Delhi Police violated the court’s October 11 order. That order directed the police not to obstruct journalists covering the anti-SIR protests, after journalists complained they were being prevented from doing their work. ‘Not a disclosure of legal authority’ The police had cited Section 172(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita to defend removing journalists “for verification”. NWMI called this “a clever use of terminology, not a disclosure of legal authority”. It said the power applies only when a person defies or ignores an earlier lawful police direction. It added that Section 29 of the Delhi Police Act, which only names the officers who can issue orders regulating assemblies and public places, is “not a freestanding authority to seize, confine or transport every person present”. The affidavit, it said, does not identify the specific direction given in each case, the rank of the officer who issued it, or what the journalist did to disobey it. Nor does it explain why removal was necessary instead of a “less restrictive measure”. As NWMI’s rejoinder stated, “The police cannot justify an interference with personal liberty simply by refraining from calling it a detention or arrest.” Reel-makers – ‘A retrospective justification’ The police had argued that protections do not extend to “reel-makers” and content creators. NWMI called the label “a retrospective justification”. “A reel is a short-form vertical-video format… not a legal or professional status,” it said. “The relevant question is what the person was doing,” the rejoinder added. NWMI also called the police’s position contradictory. items.title: Bulldozers, chainsaws and ‘parkification’: What’s happening to Delhi’s Central Ridge
items.summary: It's almost a miracle that a sprawling forest exists in the heart of Delhi. Often called the “green lungs of Delhi”, the Central Ridge is an important source of biodiversity in a city increasingly swallowed by urbanisation and smoke. But this forest, tucked away behind Rashtrapati Bhawan, now faces a different kind of threat. According to environmentalist and filmmaker Pradip Krishen, it comes from the government's own intervention. Newslaundry met the author of Trees of Delhi: A Field Guide a week before Diwali to understand what is happening to the forest. The sound of a chainsaw accompanied our conversation for nearly two hours. As we began our morning walk through Budh Jayanti Park, we spotted a JCB standing idle. By the end of our interview, it was at work. Its driver and assistants told us they had been tasked with removing two invasive species: Vilayati Keekar and Subabul . Both grow rapidly and inhibit the growth of other species. The government’s stated aim, then, is forest restoration. But for Krishen, the concern is less about what the forest department is removing than how it is going about it. Instead of being removed individually, the trees are being cleared with a bulldozer. The one we saw in action drove over the forest floor, tearing out not just invasive trees but also other vegetation in its path. The government is also attempting what Krishen calls “parkification” of the Ridge. Watch our interview to understand what this means for Delhi’s forests. items.title: The case for fast-tracking reforms in India to recognise emergency arbitration in statute
items.summary: Recognition of emergency arbitration in India's Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 requires a straightforward legislative amendment consistent with already established case law and international precedent which would demonstrate India's continued commitment to becoming a leading hub for international arbitration. As two years have passed since the Ministry of Justice published the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill 2024 for public comment, we make the case for prioritising enactment of the parts of the draft that relate to emergency arbitration, to signal India's commitment to driving the uptake of international arbitration. The Amendment Bill The stated purposes of India's Arbitration Amendment Bill are threefold: strengthen dispute resolution, reduce court interventions in arbitration and ensure the timely conclusion of arbitration proceedings. Development of the law to recognise and facilitate emergency arbitration assists with achieving all three of those goals: it helps to afford expeditious interim relief to parties awaiting constitution of an arbitral tribunal, which in turn decongests civil courts. It also enhances the effectiveness and efficiency of the arbitral process. But the Arbitration Amendment Bill remains in cold storage: it is a consultation draft and has not yet progressed to become a parliamentary bill in any form. What is the way forward? One difficulty with enacting the proposed changes to recognise emergency arbitration is that those amendments are in the same Arbitration Amendment Bill as more controversial and ambiguous changes, like the establishment of appellate arbitral tribunals. These proposed amendments raise big questions including whether or not the limited ability to appeal awards should remain vested solely in national courts as a question requiring scrutiny in the public domain, or whether such questions can legitimately be privatised. However, a consultation draft is exactly that: made for public comment and discussion,and the final form of any draft Amendment Bill may look entirely different from the initial one after public consultation. items.title: Train young lawyers: Justice Manmeet Arora urges law firms cutting costs with AI
items.summary: Delhi High Court Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora urged law firms not to stop recruiting fresh law graduates to save costs amid the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI), warning that the legal profession cannot afford to stop training its next generation of lawyers. Speaking at the first meeting of the Indian Commercial Litigators' Forum (CLF), hosted by JSA Advocates and Solicitors in New Delhi on November 20, Justice Arora asked: "We can't have a system where we only take on people after they have gained experience for three years. Who's going to train them for three years?" Justice Arora said that she had heard that some law firms in India had stopped hiring A0 associates, even as concerns grow over the potential impact of AI on employment opportunities for young lawyers. "While you are saving costs, please don't cut down on our future, because if today you will not take in A0 associates, you will not have yourselves tomorrow," she said. Responding to her observation, JSA Managing Partner Amar Gupta said that firms were conscious of the need to retain training opportunities for fresh graduates even as the firm integrates AI into its operations. “So what we have in mind is to reserve some kind of work entirely without any AI aid or assistance. And that's the first-level training that we will continue to impart to our new associates who come into our firm. And that roadmap is quite clear in our minds. We have onboarded AI models and we are doing it deliberately, with some method and planning,” Gupta said. Justice Robin Knowles of the High Court of England and Wales moderated the session virtually from London. He emphasised the value of bringing insights from both the judiciary and legal practitioners to the upcoming seventh full meeting of the Standing International Forum of Commercial Courts (SIFOCC). Delhi High Court Justice Prathiba M Singh shared global figures from a recent WIPO IP Judges Forum survey in Geneva covering 146 courts and tribunals. items.title: Supreme Court Justice Joymalya Bagchi bats for dedicated AI courts to decide mutual consent divorce cases
items.summary: Supreme Court judge Justice Joymalya Bagchi on Saturday proposed the establishment of round-the-clock artificial intelligence (AI) courts to deal with mutual consent divorce cases, saying routine judicial work should be shifted away from human judges. Justice Bagchi was speaking at the Just Tech National Conclave organised by Dharmashastra National Law University at Jabalpur on the role of AI and technology in the administration of justice. " We should, in my understanding, hive off the mutual divorce cases and have 24/7 AI divorce courts so that there will be ease of access to justice and no wastage of valuable human resources on completely non-adjudicatory exercises, " he said. Justice Bagchi said the judiciary's mounting pendency necessitates technological intervention and use of AI tools. "We are sitting on a pile of over five crore cases. The judge advocated transferring routine and predictable cases, governed by established legal principles, from human judges to AI adjudication. He said applications seeking early hearings before the Supreme Court and High Courts should also be handled through AI systems rather than judges. "This should be completely taken away from the human agency, " he said. Justice Bagchi suggested developing AI tools that could assess case pendency, optimal disposal timelines, age and other relevant considerations, including cases involving women, before deciding early hearing requests. items.title: The right to protest in the age of surveillance: Can dissent remain free under the digital gaze?
items.summary: A democracy is tested not merely by the freedoms it grants its citizens, but by the extent to which it allows them to exercise those freedoms without fear. The right to protest is among the most visible expressions of a constitutional democracy. Yet, in an age where technology can identify, track and digitally profile individuals with unprecedented precision, the very act of exercising this right may expose citizens to a different form of State scrutiny. On November 3, 2026, a petition before the Supreme Court challenged the use of CCTV cameras and facial recognition technology by the State to monitor, identify and track individuals participating in public protests. The Supreme Court issued notice on the petition , bringing into focus the constitutional question of whether participation in a public protest can justify State surveillance and the processing of individuals' personal data. Historical evolution of the right to protest in India At Independence, India inherited a colonial administrative and policing structure in which public assemblies and political demonstrations were frequently subjected to executive control. The adoption of the Constitution marked a fundamental departure from this relationship. Citizens became constitutional rights-holders, entitled to question authority and collectively express dissent. Although the Constitution does not expressly enumerate a separate fundamental right to protest, its foundations lie in Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 19(1)(c), which guarantee freedom of speech and expression, the right to assemble peacefully and without arms and the right to form associations. These freedoms collectively enable organised dissent and democratic participation, subject to the reasonable restrictions permitted by the Constitution. The Emergency of 1975–77 exposed the vulnerability of these freedoms when executive power escapes effective constitutional restraint. Restrictions on the press, preventive detention, arrests of political opponents and suppression of dissent demonstrated how quickly democratic participation could be curtailed. In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), the Supreme Court's majority denied the availability of judicial enforcement of personal liberty through habeas corpus during the Emergency under the prevailing legal framework. items.title: AI detectors incorrectly flag essays of non-native English speakers; students should not be penalised: CJI Surya Kant
items.summary: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Saturday said students should not be held guilty of academic misconduct solely on the basis of software that identifies their work as AI-generated. He cited a 2023 study which found that seven widely used AI detectors incorrectly flagged more than three in five essays by non-native English speakers as machine-generated. “ In a Commonwealth where so many students write in English as a second or third language, an honest student could thus be branded a cheat on the strength of a number that no one can explain, and that student cannot meaningfully challenge. No student should therefore be held guilty of misconduct on the word of a machine alone ,” he cautioned. The Chief Justice was delivering the inaugural address at the Commonwealth Legal Education Association’s (CLEA) first Annual International Conference on Legal Education in Hyderabad. CJI Kant further went on to oppose a blanket ban on generative AI in legal education, calling it neither practical nor wise. “ A ban (on AI) would only drive this use out of sight, where it can be neither guided nor examined. The wiser course is to set clear rules and to teach responsible use, so that technology assists the student’s search ,” he explained. Students should be told before an assessment which uses of AI are permitted, which require disclosure and which would mean handing over the thinking they are expected to do themselves, he added. He also called for changes to how students are assessed. “ Assessment, too, must evolve, so that written work is supported by an oral explanation, a defence of the authorities relied upon, or an exercise in spotting the errors in a machine-generated answer ,” the CJI suggested. Turning to practical training, he warned against internship certificates issued without attendance and clinical grades awarded for work never done. “ An internship certificate issued to a student who never attended chambers, or a clinical grade awarded for work that was never done, fails not only that student but every client he or she will one day represent ,” he remarked. CJI Kant further proposed making a minimum period of legal aid work a condition for graduation. “ I would further suggest that a minimum period of legal aid work be made compulsory for every student to graduate, with additional credits for those who go beyond it, ” he said. items.summary: The Delhi High Court has quashed criminal defamation proceedings initiated against Senior Advocate and former Biju Janata Dal (BJD) Member of Parliament Pinaki Misra for calling a lawyer a “crook”. In an order passed on November 17, Justice Sachin Datta observed that the complainant, advocate Siddhartha Singh, had failed to show that Misra's statement lowered his reputation in the estimation of others. The Court allowed Misra' plea and set aside the summoning order passed by a trial court in April 2019 as well as the complaint filed by Singh. "It is also noticed that the impugned order does not consider the context in which the words were allegedly used by the petitioner and the dismissal of the complaint by the Bar Council of Delhi," the Court said. The case arose from an August 2018 report published by The Economic Times about a complaint filed by Singh before the Bar Council of Delhi, alleging professional misconduct by Misra over a conflict of interest. At the time, Misra was a Lok Sabha MP and chairperson of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Urban Development. Singh had objected to Misra appearing for power distribution companies before the National Green Tribunal, claiming that the committee chaired by him had made adverse recommendations against the companies. The newspaper report quoted Misra as allegedly calling Singh a “crook”. Singh then sent a legal notice to Misra seeking an unconditional apology before filing the criminal defamation complaint. After considering the case, Justice Datta noted that Singh had examined only himself as a witness before the trial court and had not named or examined anyone who had read the report or whose estimation of him had been affected. The Court also noted that the Bar Council had dismissed Singh's professional misconduct complaint in November 2018. It further pointed out that a connected defamation case arising from a report published on Daily Hunt had already been quashed by the High Court in August 2026. Senior Advocate Rebecca M John along with advocate Anushka Baruah appeared for Pinaki Misra. Senior Advocate Rebecca John Additional Public Prosecutor (APP) Aashneet Singh appeared for the State. items.title: Women in high public office does not mean equality has been achieved: Justice BV Nagarathna at Oxford
items.summary: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna recently said that the presence of women in high public offices does not mean equality has been achieved across the society. She added that even a guaranteed right can be difficult to exercise in practice due to cost, delay and social consequences. "The existence of women in high public office does not establish that equality has been achieved throughout society. A woman may hold a senior position while other women remain excluded from education, employment, property, or effective legal remedies," the judge said. The judge made the comment while delivering the inaugural Cornelia Sorabji Memorial Lecture at the Oxford India Centre for Sustainable Development in Somerville College, University of Oxford, on November 18. The lecture was on the topic "The Doors She Opened: Cornelia Sorabji and the Progress of Women's Rights in India." Justice BV Nagarathna A woman may hold a senior position while other women remain excluded from education, employment, property, or effective legal remedies. The judge said the progress of women's rights cannot be measured only by the number of discriminatory provisions struck down or beneficial statutes enacted. On violence against women, she said the challenge "cannot be overcome by simply enacting more laws." She also highlighted the burden of unpaid domestic and care work and the differences among women arising from caste, class, disability, religion and region. Specifically on the legal profession, Justice Nagarathna spoke about reservation for women lawyers. "I have consistently advocated for one-third reservation for women lawyers on government panels, including those representing public sector undertakings and in the sphere of legal aid, " she said. She added that the representation must go beyond the right to enter the profession and include opportunities to represent the State, advise public institutions and participate in the exercise of legal authority. items.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed the Karnataka government's appeal challenging the Karnataka High Court's decision to allow bike taxi services to operate in the State. A Bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh passed the ruling. By this ruling, a Divison Bench of the High Court effectively lifted a court-ordered ban on bike taxi services in the State. The Bench of Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice CM Joshi allowed appeals filed by aggregators including Ola, Uber and Rapido against an earlier order suspending bike taxi operations until Karnataka framed a regulatory policy. A single judge of the Court had earlier ordered that bike taxi services be halted until the State comes out with a policy permitting the same. This ruling was challenged in appeals filed by Ola, Uber, Rapido, motorcycle owners and the Bike Taxi Welfare Association. Karnataka subsequently approached the Supreme Court, raising concerns over passenger safety, insurance coverage and the absence of adequate safeguards for bike taxi passengers. items.title: Kerala HC allows RSS-linked teachers' body to hold exam in state schools
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Friday, November 20, permitted a teachers’ organisation affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) to conduct its district-level Young Scholar Exam 2026 in government and aided schools across the state on November 22. The interim order comes despite the state government withdrawing its earlier permission for the examination, following allegations that it could be used to propagate Hindu nationalist ideology among schoolchildren. The examination is being organised by the National Teachers’ Union (NTU), Kerala, the state unit of the Akhil Bharatiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh (ABRSM), a teachers’ organisation associated with the Sangh Parivar. It is being conducted in association with Mayilpeeli, a children's magazine published by Balagokulam, an organisation linked to the RSS and known for organising Sree Krishna Jayanti celebrations in Kerala. The involvement of these organisations triggered a political controversy after the General Education Department initially permitted the examination to be conducted in government and aided schools. Justice Gopinath P issued the interim order on a petition filed by T Anoop Kumar, general secretary of Deshiya Adhyapaka Parishath (NTU) Kerala, challenging the General Education Department's November 14 order withdrawing the permission granted earlier. While allowing the examination to proceed as scheduled, the court restrained the organisers from publishing its results or conducting any further examinations without obtaining additional orders from the court. “Since all arrangements have been made for conduct of the examination on 22.11.2026, there will be an interim order directing that the petitioner shall be permitted to conduct the examination,” the court said. The order further clarified: “The petitioner/the organization conducting the examination shall not declare any results of the examination and shall not conduct any further examination, without obtaining further orders from this Court.” The dispute arose after the Director of General Education granted permission to NTU on October 12 to conduct the Young Scholar Exam 2026 for students from Classes 5 to 10 in government and aided schools. The approval was subsequently withdrawn following complaints and political criticism, with General Education Minister N Samsudheen directing the department to revoke the permission. items.title: Padmaja Venugopal apologises to Congress workers, says she wants to rejoin party
items.summary: Padmaja Venugopal, daughter of former Kerala chief minister and Congress veteran K Karunakaran, has apologised to Congress workers for joining the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in 2024. The apology comes amid growing opposition within the Congress to her proposed return to the party following her exit from the BJP on November 19. In a Facebook post on Saturday, November 21, Padmaja said she had realised that her decision to join the BJP had deeply hurt Congress workers who were fond of both her and her father. She said she was preparing to return after recognising the impact her departure had on the party and its workers. “When I said, while resigning, that joining the BJP was a wrong decision I had made in an emotional moment, I was speaking from my heart. I realised that the decision I had taken back then deeply hurt many Congress workers who loved both K Karunakaran and me. It was this realisation that prompted me to prepare for a return,” she said. Stating that she was not aspiring for any position within the party, Padmaja said her only wish was to become a Congress worker again. She also acknowledged the criticism directed at her by Congress workers from different parts of the state and apologised for the hurt caused by her decision. “I fully acknowledge and accept the criticism levelled against me by Congress workers from various quarters. I would also like to use this opportunity to sincerely apologise, from the bottom of my heart, to every Congress worker and to the party for the hurt my decision caused,” she said. Padmaja added that her immediate aim was to pay her respects at her father's memorial alongside Congress workers on his death anniversary next month. Her statement comes a day after reports emerged that she had contacted Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) president Sunny Joseph and expressed her wish to return to the party. Sunny confirmed the phone conversation but said the Congress had not received a formal request from her. He said the matter had not been discussed at the party level and that a decision would be taken after consultations with the leadership. Her proposed return has, however, triggered opposition from sections of the Congress, particularly younger leaders who have questioned whether she has adequately addressed the political positions she took against the party before joining the BJP. items.summary: University of Hyderabad students have launched an indefinite protest demanding the termination of Dr Vijaya Ramdas Mandala, a faculty member in the History Department, over his alleged derogatory remarks about Dalit students in an email exchange. The remarks were allegedly made after a former student expressed hesitation regarding incorporating certain suggestions made by Vijaya Ramdas into his research because of ethical concerns. items.title: Belonging: Sonia Gandhi’s memoir is from the heart, moving but playing it safe
items.summary: The picture in your head, as you read Sonia Gandhi's Belonging , can at first be black and white and grainy like the front cover, of her young face looking at an India of nearly 60 years ago, when she first came here for love. The picture gathers colour as you read on and find Sonia at home in India, slowly and almost hesitatingly growing into the Congress veteran she has become. Just like in politics, she seems to have inadvertently captured her extraordinary life, without really wanting to, in her from-the-heart memoir. The book, selling like it had been awaited forever, though it was announced only earlier this year, may have that kind of pull because it comes from one of India’s most important political figures. But it is her writing that sustains that pull and keeps the reader turning the pages. When nonfiction has this kind of effect it is lazily lauded as reading like fiction. But Sonia’s life, overwhelmed with untoward incidents, could easily have become a chaotic mess on paper. One has to imagine that it is her artistic bent of mind (she writes about losing herself in museums) that brought order to the writing, placing in forefront the personal life that almost helplessly slips into the political. The way she begins makes you wonder if she simply dived into her past and picked up her first memory of Rajiv Gandhi and their meeting in an English cafe. She was 19, he 21, just bereaved of his grandfather Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister of India. But Nehru and Indira Gandhi, Rajiv’s mother and yet another Prime Minister-to-be, do not come into the picture until later. Sonia keeps it personal for many pages, almost cheesily so, describing their days of courtship and her feelings for the young and handsome man, who at times, lost his temper. She details her childhood, growing up in fear of her disciplinarian dad, who can seem like an Amrish Puri of Indian Cinema, only he is in Orbassano of Italy, towering over his subdued wife and three daughters.
